newsitem.title: MALDIVES: South Asian leaders for opening political dialogue.
newsitem.headline: South Asian leaders for opening political dialogue.

text.p: South Asian leaders may open the door to political dialogue within the region's seven-nation bloc, ending a ban on the discussion of such matters, a Maldivian government minister said on Tuesday.

Tourism Minister Ibrahim Hussain Zaki said in an interview that the leaders of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC), meeting on this Indian Ocean island state, might agree to start political dialogue among themselves.

"Political dialogue might come in the declaration and that will be a major breakthrough," Zaki said about the proposal that was moved by Maldivian President Maumoon Abdul Gayoom on Monday at the opening of a SAARC summit in Male.

SAARC groups Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Pakistan with a goal of accelerating economic growth in the region of about 1.2 billion people, more than 500 million of whom live in poverty.
The SAARC leaders aim to issue a joint declaration at the end of the summit on Wednesday.

SAARC, long burdened by disputes between member nations, especially India and Pakistan, has no formal framework to tackle bilateral quarrels. The 12-year-old organisation's charter bars members from bringing up bilateral matters at meetings.
Some critics say the bloc will never become a truly integrated economic zone until its member states can also deal together with sensitive political matters.
"We (should) institute a separate but parallel process of political dialogue, for the purpose of further consolidating understanding and harmony amongst our countries," Gayoom had said.
"We must take this step because regional peace and stability (are) far too important to be left unattended," he told a ceremony on Monday opening the three-day SAARC summit.
The prime ministers of India and Pakistan on Monday held bilateral talks on a resort island in the Maldives, but the meeting was outside of SAARC.

In her speech at the SAARC inauguration on Monday, Sri Lankan President Chandrika Bandaranaike Kumaratunga said the bloc's achievements had been "relatively insubstantial", stymied by a lack of political will and common vision.

The Sri Lankan leader called for "frequent, informal and confidential, free and frank interlocution amongst ourselves...dispelling suspicions and arriving hopefully in time at shared perceptions about ourselves and our region".
Zaki said the seven nations would be better placed to resolve problems if they could engage in political dialogue.

"If they can sit down together and speak about a common problem, a problem which is faced either by one state or two states, then of course there is a collective wisdom that comes into play," Zaki said.
He said there was this growing sense among leaders that time was being lost and they were determined to revitalise SAARC.

"For the first time, directly or indirectly, the leaders have confessed the time of lost opportunity cost is too high. Time is running out, they have to be serious, they have to put their acts together, otherwise they will be marginalised," he said.
"We are prepared now to commit. Let us do something solid."
